newsitem.title: GERMANY: German soldiers struggle to stop Oder dike burst.
newsitem.headline: German soldiers struggle to stop Oder dike burst.

text.p: German authorities were hopeful on Thursday that they would be able to stop a dike on River Oder from breaking open and flooding homes and crops but said the situation was still tense.

Around 10,000 residents of the Oder valley region were evacuated late on Wednesday, after the dike near the village of Hohenwutzen collapsed under the weight of two weeks of floods that have ravaged Poland and the Czech Republic. Just under 5,000 people had been evacuated from the region last week.
"The situation has improved slightly," said Peter Salendar, spokesman for the crisis committee in Bad Freienwalde.
"Soldiers are now able to work directly on the dike and that is a good sign, but the situation is still critical."

Some of the worst floods this century have hit Poland and the Czech Republic this month, claiming more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.
At one point during the evening, soldiers were taken off the dike because the work had become too dangerous and helicopters flew in tonnes of sand in an effort to stabilise the barrier.
The spokesman denied reports that water had flowed into the village of Hohenwutzen, but said a large pool of water had gathered at the foot of the dike where it was seeping through.

Brandenburg state government officials were divided about the chances of saving the dike. The Interior Ministry thought the chances of the dike holding were 50-50, but state Environment Minister Matthias Platzeck was less optimistic.
"The chance that it will hold are around 10 percent," he said. "In any event we will have to work on it for the next 24 hours."

In the villages below the main barrier still holding back the swelling Oder that divides Germany and Poland, families had packed what they could carry in their cars and left their homes, not knowing when they would return.

The Oderbruch region, once the bread basket of the former communist East Germany, was drained 250 years ago by King Frederick the Great of Prussia to create fertile farmland. It is vulnerable to flooding because it lies lower than the river, which is held back by dikes.
Farmers gathered cattle, pigs and sheep to be transported out of the region, taken to higher ground for safety. Should the dike break there will be extensive damage to homes, businesses and crops.
Brandenburg Premier Manfred Stolpe estimated the damages so far at around one billion marks ($544.1 million).
Most of the damage is south of Frankfurt an der Oder, some 70 km (45 miles) east of Berlin. In the villages of Wiesenau and Ziltendorf more than 100 homes are still under water.
Officials will begin inoculations this week as a preventive measure to ward off any diseases from the rotting carcasses of dead animals caught helplessly in the rushing stream.
On Wednesday the European Union proposed 1.5 million Ecus ($1.6 million) in relief aid for the state of Brandenburg to help the battered region cope with the flooding. ($ = 1.837 German Marks)
